x.ASV: A Psalm of Asaph. God standeth in the congregation of God; He judgeth among the gods.
x.Darby: A Psalm of Asaph. God standeth in the assembly ofGod, he judgeth among thegods.
x.KJV: A Psalm of Asaph. God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.
x.YLT: --A Psalm of Asaph. God hath stood in the company of God, In the midst God doth judge.

nt: The expression **is standing** was a common expression meaning to take one’s position of authority in order to act. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [takes his position of authority]
The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [in the midst of the spirit beings]

x.ASV: How long will ye judge unjustly, And respect the persons of the wicked? [Selah
x.Darby: How long will ye judge unrighteously, and accept the person of the wicked? Selah.
x.KJV: How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.
x.YLT: Till when do ye judge perversely? And the face of the wicked lift up? Selah.

nt: Asaph is using the question form to rebuke these judges for their corrupt rulings. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for this purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [You must stop judging with injustice and stop making rulings that favor the wicked!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **injustice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [unjustly]

The expression **lift up the faces of the wicked** was a common expression meaning “to show partiality or favoritism.” If it would be helpful for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and show partiality to wicked people]

Asaph is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are wicked]

x.ASV: Judge the poor and fatherless: Do justice to the afflicted and destitute.
x.Darby: Judge the poor and the fatherless, do justice to the afflicted and the destitute;
x.KJV: Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
x.YLT: Judge ye the weak and fatherless, The afflicted and the poor declare righteous.

nt: Asaph is using the adjectives **poor**, **orphan**, and **destitute** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the poor people and the fatherless children; vindicate the poor people and the destitute people]

x.ASV: Rescue the poor and needy: Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.
x.Darby: Rescue the poor and needy, deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.
x.KJV: Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.
x.YLT: Let the weak and needy escape, From the hand of the wicked deliver them.

nt: Asaph is using the adjectives **poor**, **needy**, and **wicked** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the poor people and the needy people; deliver them from the hand of the wicked people]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of the wicked people]

x.ASV: They know not, neither do they understand; They walk to and fro in darkness: All the foundations of the earth are shaken.
x.Darby: They know not, neither do they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are moved.
x.KJV: They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.
x.YLT: They knew not, nor do they understand, In darkness they walk habitually, Moved are all the foundations of earth.

nt: The terms **do not know** and **do not understand** mean similar things. Asaph is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They are completely ignorant]

Asaph is speaking of these judges as if they were walking around in a dark place. He means that they are morally ignorant and do not act according to what is right. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation, or you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they go about in moral ignorance]

Asaph is speaking of the moral and social order of the world as if it had **foundations** like those under a building. He means that because of these unjust judges, the stability of the world is being destroyed. You may have a comparable expression in your language that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All the stability and order of the world is being undermined]

The phrase **are shaken** is a passive verbal form. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [shake] or [are trembling]

x.ASV: I said, Ye are gods, And all of you sons of the Most High.
x.Darby: I have said, Ye aregods, and all of you are children of the Most High;
x.KJV: I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.
x.YLT: I--I have said, `Gods ye are, And sons of the Most High--all of you,

nt: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. In that case, you could express what God said as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [I said that you are gods]

Asaph is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one speaking. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself said]
See the discussion of the term “gods” in the introduction to this psalm.

Asaph is speaking of these judges as if they were **sons of the Most High**, that is, as if they belonged to God’s family. He means that God had given them a share in his authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and those who share the authority of the Most High]

x.ASV: Nevertheless ye shall die like men, And fall like one of the princes.
x.Darby: But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.
x.KJV: But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.
x.YLT: But as man ye die, and as one of the heads ye fall,

nt: Asaph uses the word **But** here to introduce a contrast between the divine status declared in the previous verse and the mortality declared here. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However,]

The point of this comparison is that despite being called gods, these judges will die just as any ordinary human person does. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point clear. Alternate translation: [like any mortal person, you will die]

The point of this comparison is that these judges will lose their position and power just as earthly rulers do when they are defeated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like any other ruler, you will fall from power]

x.ASV: Arise, O God, judge the earth; For thou shalt inherit all the nations.
x.Darby: Arise, OGod, judge the earth; for thou shalt inherit all the nations.
x.KJV: Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.
x.YLT: Rise, O God, judge the earth, For Thou hast inheritance among all the nations!

nt: Asaph is using the imperative forms **Arise** and **judge** to make a request of God. If your language does not use the imperative to make requests, you could express this as a request or wish. Alternate translation: [Please arise, God, and judge the earth]

The word translated as **you** before **you will inherit** represents an independent pronoun used for emphasis in the original language, in addition to the pronoun expressed within the verb. If it would be helpful in your language, you could indicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you yourself will inherit]

Asaph is speaking of God’s sovereign ownership and authority over the nations as if God would **inherit** them as property. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you possess authority over all the nations]

Asaph is giving a reason for what he said in the previous phrase. He asked God to judge the earth and he now gives the reason: God possesses authority over all the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this connection more explicit. Alternate translation: [because you have authority over all the nations]
